bib.title: Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning, Chapter 2: Probability Distributions

read.skipped: Nothing skipped. Chapter pages 67-136 plus exercises 2.1-2.61 read to end of text; the cached text ends with exercise 2.61 (no references in this extract).

question: Which standard probability distributions (binomial, multinomial, Gaussian, exponential family) and density estimators serve as building blocks for pattern recognition, and how do frequentist and Bayesian parameter inference work on them?
contributions: Conjugate-prior Bayesian inference worked through for Bernoulli/Beta, multinomial/Dirichlet, Gaussian mean, Gaussian precision (Gamma), and Gaussian mean+precision (normal-gamma, normal-Wishart).
Closed-form conditional, marginal and Bayes-theorem results for partitioned and linear-Gaussian models.
Exponential family, sufficient statistics, conjugate priors and noninformative priors in general form.
Nonparametric density estimation: histograms, kernels (Parzen), K nearest neighbours and K-NN classification.

results.claim: Maximum likelihood on 3 coin flips giving 3 heads sets mu_ML to 1, predicting all future flips heads; the book calls this extreme over-fitting.
results.setup: Bernoulli likelihood, N=3 flips, m=3 heads, no prior
results.quote: N = m = 3 and µML = 1

results.claim: One sequential Bayesian step: a Beta(2,2) prior plus one observation of x=1 gives a Beta(3,2) posterior (a incremented by m, b by l).
results.setup: Beta prior a=2,b=2; binomial likelihood N=m=1
results.quote: with parameters a = 3, b = 2.

results.claim: Bayesian predictive probability of heads with a Beta(a,b) prior is (m+a)/(m+a+l+b), the fraction of real plus fictitious observations; it equals the ML estimate as m,l go to infinity.
results.setup: Bernoulli/binomial with Beta prior, i.i.d. data
results.quote: reduces to the maximum likelihood result (2.8)

results.setup: General Bayesian inference for parameter theta

results.claim: The ML covariance estimate of a Gaussian is biased: E[Sigma_ML] = (N-1)/N Sigma; the estimator with 1/(N-1) is unbiased, while mu_ML is unbiased.
results.setup: Multivariate Gaussian, N i.i.d. samples, joint ML in mu and Sigma
results.quote: an expectation that is less than the true value, and hence it is biased

results.claim: A full-covariance D-dimensional Gaussian has D(D+3)/2 free parameters, so parameters grow quadratically in D.
results.setup: General symmetric Sigma: D(D+1)/2 plus D for the mean
results.quote: D(D + 3)/2 parameters in total

results.claim: An isotropic covariance Sigma = sigma^2 I has D+1 parameters (a diagonal covariance has 2D).
results.setup: Gaussian with Sigma = sigma^2 I
results.quote: giving D + 1 independent parameters in the model

results.claim: Gaussian posterior for the mean (known variance): posterior precision = prior precision + N/sigma^2; posterior mean is a precision-weighted compromise between prior mean and sample mean.
results.setup: Univariate Gaussian, known sigma^2, Gaussian prior N(mu0, sigma0^2)
results.quote: the precisions are additive

results.claim: The sequential ML mean update mu_N = mu_{N-1} + (1/N)(x_N - mu_{N-1}) is the Robbins-Monro procedure with a_N = sigma^2/N.
results.setup: Gaussian mean, z = (x - mu_ML)/sigma^2
results.quote: to have the form aN = σ2/N

results.claim: Robbins-Monro step sizes must satisfy a_N -> 0, sum a_N = infinity, sum a_N^2 < infinity for convergence with probability one.
results.setup: Root finding of a regression function f(theta)=E[z|theta], finite conditional variance
results.quote: converge to the root with probability one

results.claim: Student's t is an infinite mixture of Gaussians with the same mean and Gamma-distributed precisions; nu=1 gives the Cauchy and nu to infinity the Gaussian; mean exists for nu>1 and covariance nu/(nu-2) Lambda^-1 for nu>2.
results.setup: Univariate/multivariate Student t, Gaussian N(x|mu,tau^-1) with Gam(tau|a,b), nu=2a, lambda=a/b
results.quote: For the particular case of ν = 1, the t-distribution reduces

results.claim: Student t ML fit is far less distorted by 3 outliers than a Gaussian ML fit (30 Gaussian draws plus 3 outliers).
results.setup: 30 points from a Gaussian, with and without 3 added outliers; t fitted by EM (Exercise 12.24)
results.quote: distribution of 30 data points drawn from a Gaussian distribution

results.claim: Treating angles as ordinary numbers is origin dependent: for observations at 1 and 359 degrees, origin 0 gives mean 180 and std 179, origin 180 gives mean 0 and std 1.
results.setup: Two angles theta1=1 deg, theta2=359 deg, univariate Gaussian
results.quote: will be 180◦with standard deviation 179◦

results.claim: A single Gaussian cannot capture the two clumps of the Old Faithful data (272 measurements); a mixture of two Gaussians does.
results.setup: Old Faithful: eruption duration (min) vs time to next eruption (min); single ML Gaussian vs two-component mixture fitted by ML (Chapter 9)
results.quote: comprises 272 measurements of the eruption of the Old Faithful geyser
results.note: Counts only; no fit quality is reported.

results.claim: With a mixture of Gaussians the log likelihood has a sum inside the log, so no closed-form ML solution exists; use numerical optimisation or EM (Chapter 9).
results.setup: Gaussian mixture, log likelihood sum_n ln sum_k pi_k N(x_n|mu_k,Sigma_k)
results.quote: no longer has a closed-form analytical solution

results.claim: Noninformative priors: a location parameter gets a constant prior, a scale parameter gets p(sigma) proportional to 1/sigma (constant in ln sigma); the Gamma prior with a0=b0=0 is the noninformative limit for a precision.
results.setup: Location/scale families; both priors improper
results.quote: and hence p(σ) ∝1/σ.

results.claim: Histogram density estimation with bin width Delta: p_i = n_i/(N Delta_i); the number of bins is M^D for M bins in D dimensions (curse of dimensionality).
results.setup: Equal-width bins, D-dimensional space, M bins per variable
results.quote: then the total number of bins will be M D

results.claim: Kernel and K-NN density estimators converge to the true density as N->infinity provided V shrinks suitably with N and K grows with N.
results.setup: Both estimators from p(x)=K/(NV)
results.quote: provided V shrinks suitably with N, and K grows with N (Duda and Hart, 1973)

results.claim: K-NN classification posterior is p(C_k|x)=K_k/K; the K=1 rule has asymptotic error at most twice the Bayes-optimal error.
results.setup: Nearest-neighbour rule, limit N->infinity, true class distributions known for the optimal classifier
results.quote: the error rate is never more than twice the minimum achievable error

results.claim: Oil-flow K-NN example uses 200 data points, features x6 vs x7 and K = 1, 3, 31; small K gives many small regions, large K fewer larger regions.
results.setup: Oil flow data (Chapter 1), classes laminar/annular/homogeneous, K-NN decision regions
results.quote: Plot of 200 data points from the oil data set

results.claim: Kernel density and K-NN estimators need the whole training set stored; kernel evaluation cost grows linearly with data set size and the K-NN model is not a true density (integral diverges).
results.setup: Kernel density estimator (2.249); K-NN (2.246)
results.quote: is not a true density model because the integral over all space diverges

limits: Parametric distributions assume a fixed functional form; the Gaussian is unimodal and its parameters grow as D(D+3)/2 (p.83-84).
Density estimation is stated to be fundamentally ill-posed: infinitely many distributions fit a finite data set (p.67-68).
Nonparametric methods store the whole data set; histograms scale as M^D bins; K-NN is not a normalised density; the authors say these remain severely limited (p.121-127).
Posterior-variance shrinkage holds only on average (p.74).
Figure illustrations (2.12, 2.16, 2.24-2.28) are qualitative and give no error metrics; no experiments with reported accuracy appear in the chapter.
Nonparametric Bayesian methods (Dirichlet processes etc.) are only cited, not covered (p.120).
Inverse gamma and inverse Wishart priors are mentioned but not developed (p.101-102).
practices: Use the 1-of-K encoding for a discrete variable with K states (p.74-75).
Put a Beta (or Dirichlet) prior on Bernoulli (multinomial) parameters; read a and b (alpha_k) as effective counts of prior observations (p.71-72, 77).
Avoid raw ML for small samples: ML on 3 flips with 3 heads gives mu=1 (p.70).
Work with the precision (inverse variance) when doing Bayesian inference for a Gaussian (p.99-101).
Use the unbiased covariance estimator with 1/(N-1) rather than the ML 1/N (p.94, Eq 2.125).
Use a heavy-tailed Student t instead of a Gaussian when outliers or mislabelled data are likely; this also makes regression more robust (p.103-104).
Do not apply a Gaussian to periodic variables such as angles; use unit-vector averaging or the von Mises distribution (p.105-109).
Use mixtures of Gaussians for multimodal or clumped data such as Old Faithful (p.110-111).
Use a sequential (online) update, e.g. Robbins-Monro, when data arrive as a stream or are too large for batch processing (p.73, 94-97).
Choose the smoothing parameter (bin width, kernel h, or K) at an intermediate value, treating it as a model-complexity choice (p.121-125).
Use a noninformative prior only after checking parameterisation: a constant prior is not invariant under nonlinear reparametrisation; use 1/sigma for scale parameters (p.118-120).
For K-NN classification take the majority class among the K nearest points and break ties at random (p.126).

a prior that leads to a posterior having the same functional form as the prior

parameters (a, b) that control the distribution of the parameter mu
Delta^2 = (x-mu)^T Sigma^-1 (x-mu); reduces to Euclidean distance when Sigma is the identity
the inverse of the covariance matrix, Lambda = Sigma^-1
a matrix whose eigenvalues are strictly positive
a Gaussian whose mean is a linear function of the conditioning variable with covariance independent of it
sequential root-finding theta_N = theta_{N-1} + a_{N-1} z(theta_{N-1}) for a regression function f(theta)=E[z|theta]
periodic Gaussian-like density p(theta|theta0,m) = exp{m cos(theta-theta0)}/(2 pi I0(m)); m is the concentration
posterior probabilities p(k|x) of mixture components
distributions of the form p(x|eta)=h(x) g(eta) exp(eta^T u(x))
a prior whose integral diverges, e.g. constant over an unbounded domain
mu in p(x|mu)=f(x-mu); sigma in p(x|sigma)=(1/sigma) f(x/sigma)
fix K and grow a sphere around x until it holds K points; p(x)=K/(NV)

problems: Text extraction drops many math symbols and fraction layout; formulas were checked against surrounding prose, not rendered. Ligature characters (fi, fl) appear in the cached text, so quotes were taken from lines without them.
Eq 2.243 prints P^K (1-P)^{1-K}; the exponent should be N-K (typo in printed text).
Eq 2.250 prints the Gaussian kernel normaliser (2 pi h^2)^{1/2}; for D dimensions it should be (2 pi h^2)^{D/2}, as the text uses D elsewhere.
Eq 2.87 last line as extracted shows (Lambda_aa - Lambda_ab Lambda_bb^-1 Lambda_ba)^-1 mu_a with a -1 power, but 2.89 uses it without the inverse; likely a print typo or extraction artefact.
Notation drifts: K states (Sec 2.2) vs M (Eq 2.28 mu_M, Eq 2.204 'x=(x1..xN)', Eq 2.209, Exercise 2.9); Eq 2.28 ends at mu_M.
Exercise 2.14 says 'the maximum likelihood distribution is given by the Gaussian' where it means maximum entropy; Exercise 2.4 says 'mean of n' where the variable is m.
Text spells 'Jeffries, 1946' for Jeffreys and 'Box and Tao, 1973' for Box and Tiao.
